title: Let them come
hookLine: Jews sit shiva; some Muslim families receive mourners for three days: grief is meant to be accompanied

lines: THE HARD PART: OPENING THE DOOR.
GRIEF IS MEANT TO HAVE COMPANY.
cards: A casserole dish on a doorstep, covered in foil, with a note taped to the lid. By evening there's another. Then a bag of bagels, a tray of fruit, somebody's aunt at the door with a pot of soup.
On some streets, when there's been a death, the food starts arriving before anyone asks for it. And for the family inside, the hard part may not be cooking at all. It's opening the door.
In more than one tradition, grief is meant to have company, not a quiet house.

teach.b: First, the seven days. In Jewish tradition, after a burial, the close family sits shiva. They stay home, and the community comes to them.
The Bible already knows a seven-day mourning: when Jacob dies, Genesis says of his son Joseph, "he made a mourning for his father seven days."
Some families leave the front door unlocked during shiva, so visitors can let themselves in and the mourners don't have to get up. Second, the first meal.

teach.h: THE FIRST MEAL FROM OTHER HANDS.
teach.b: Jewish tradition, recorded in the Talmud, says the first meal after the burial should come from someone else's hands, not the mourner's own kitchen. Neighbors cook. The mourner's job is to eat.
Third, the same instinct in another house. A hadith tells of the day news came that a man named Ja'far had died.

The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, told the people to prepare food for Ja'far's family, because something had come to them that would keep them busy. It's in the collections of Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi.
In some Muslim families today, relatives and neighbors receive visitors and bring meals for three days. Fourth, the other side of the door. Every one of these customs needs two people.
Someone carries the soup up the path.

teach.h: SOMEONE HAS TO OPEN THE DOOR.
teach.b: Someone else has to open the door and take it. For a person who is used to being the helper, that second job can feel like the harder one. In these traditions, saying yes to the casserole isn't a failure at grieving.
It is part of how grieving is done.
The visitors come. The mourner lets them.

how: Jewish mourners sit shiva at home while the community visits and brings food, and in some Muslim families relatives and neighbors receive visitors and send meals for three days after a death.

gather everyone for a long speech.

practice: Bring to mind one person who has offered help you waved away, or someone who would come if you asked.
Let the door open in your mind, let them stand there with whatever they're carrying, and notice what happens when you imagine saying yes; if something tightens, breathe there.
If you pray, you can bring that person to God by name, and then simply breathe, as someone who is allowed to be cared for.

wordCard.voice: Shiva, the week a Jewish family sits at home after a burial while the community comes to them. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew, from Jewish mourning custom: the word for seven, the days the family sits at home and receives visitors.

carryVoice: Your line: someone else's hands. Even a small yes, a ride or a coffee, counts. That's day seven hundred forty-three.
